carePlan.title: Care Plan
carePlan.description: What matters most after your latest assessment.
carePlan.emptyDescription: Once you complete an assessment, your most recent diagnosis and follow-up plan will appear here.
carePlan.urgentPriorityText: Your latest result includes an urgent flag. Follow the recommendation promptly and contact a clinician if symptoms are getting worse.
carePlan.routinePriorityText: Your latest result does not show an urgent flag. Continue with the recommended follow-up and monitor any symptom changes.
carePlan.noSymptoms: No symptoms reported in your latest assessment.
carePlan.numbersNoLabs: No lab values yet — a fasting glucose and HbA1c test will make your reports far more accurate.
carePlan.understandingConfirmed: Your results meet the criteria for diabetes. This is not an emergency — it means your blood sugar has been consistently above the normal range. The next step is a care plan: meet your clinician, set sugar targets, and start treatment, plus regular eye and foot checks.
carePlan.understandingPossible: Your answers match common signs of diabetes, but a blood test is still needed to confirm. Book a fasting glucose or HbA1c test — it takes minutes and any lab can do it.
carePlan.understandingPrediabetes: Your numbers sit in the borderline range between normal and diabetes. This stage can often be reversed: about 7% weight loss, 150 minutes of activity a week, and fewer sugary drinks sharply lower the risk.
carePlan.understandingGestational: Your results relate to diabetes in pregnancy. Pregnancy changes how the body handles sugar. Your obstetric team will plan glucose monitoring and diet first — with good control, most pregnancies go well.
carePlan.understandingLowRisk: No strong diabetes signs were found in your latest assessment. Keep your healthy routines, re-check routinely every 1–3 years, and come back sooner if new symptoms appear.
carePlan.understandingType1: Your pattern (rapid onset with weight loss) fits type 1 diabetes, where the body stops making insulin. This needs specialist care quickly — insulin treatment cannot wait for a routine appointment.
carePlan.understandingMixed: Your results show features of more than one diabetes type. A clinician may order extra antibody tests to pick the right treatment.
carePlan.understandingFallback: This report compares your answers against medical rules for diabetes. Open the full report to see the evidence behind it and the recommended next steps.
carePlan.warningBody: Go to emergency care for fruity-smelling breath, deep or fast breathing, vomiting with no fluids kept down, confusion or extreme drowsiness. For shakiness, sweating or dizziness, take fast sugar (juice or glucose tablets) and recheck after 15 minutes.

recommendations.title: Recommended for you
recommendations.description: Generated automatically from your latest assessment data.
recommendations.basisUrgentFlag: urgent flag on your latest result
recommendations.urgentFollowUpText: Your latest assessment was flagged urgent. Don't wait — follow the recommendation and speak to a clinician as soon as you can.
recommendations.crisisSignsText: You reported warning signs ({{symptoms}}). These can indicate a dangerous glucose crisis — get urgent medical help immediately.
recommendations.hypoSignsTitle: Know how to treat low blood sugar
recommendations.hypoSignsText: Shakiness, sweating or dizziness can mean low blood sugar. If it happens, take fast-acting sugar (juice, glucose tablets) and tell your clinician.
recommendations.veryHighGlucoseText: A reading of {{value}} mg/dL needs medical attention soon. Contact your clinician, drink water, and avoid sugary drinks for now.
recommendations.missingLabsTitle: Add lab tests to unlock better insight
recommendations.missingLabsText: Your assessments have no lab values yet. A fasting glucose and HbA1c test would make your reports and these recommendations far more accurate.
recommendations.diabetesRangeGlucoseTitle: Discuss your glucose with a clinician
recommendations.diabetesRangeGlucoseText: Your fasting glucose of {{value}} mg/dL is in the diabetes range. Book an appointment to confirm the result and plan next steps.
recommendations.prediabetesGlucoseText: Your glucose of {{value}} mg/dL is in the warning range. Diet changes and regular movement now can bring it back to normal.
recommendations.a1cElevatedText: Your HbA1c of {{value}}% is above target. A check every 3 months shows whether your plan is actually working.
recommendations.weightManagementText: A BMI of {{value}} responds well to small changes: balanced portions and a daily walk. Even a 5% weight loss measurably improves glucose.
recommendations.underweightText: A BMI of {{value}} is below the healthy range. Focus on nutrient-rich meals and ask a professional about a safe plan to gain weight.
recommendations.symptomDiaryText: You reported {{count}} symptoms ({{symptoms}}). Note when they appear and how strong they feel — it helps your clinician spot patterns.
recommendations.quitSmokingTitle: Quit smoking to protect your vessels
recommendations.quitSmokingText: Smoking sharply raises the risk of diabetes complications. Ask your clinician about cessation support — it's one of the highest-impact changes you can make.
recommendations.reassessSoonText: Your last check was {{days}} days ago. Re-run the assessment to keep your report and trends up to date.
recommendations.bpMonitorTitle: Check your blood pressure at home
recommendations.bpMonitorText: You flagged hypertension. Measure twice a week at rest and bring the readings to your appointments.
recommendations.yearlyScreeningText: Your risk factors make yearly glucose checks important — even when you feel completely fine.
recommendations.buildHistoryText: You've completed {{count}} assessment(s). Repeating the assessment monthly reveals trends and makes every report smarter.
recommendations.stayActiveText: Brisk walking, cycling or swimming lowers glucose and improves insulin sensitivity. Start with 10-minute walks after meals.
recommendations.balancedDietText: Half vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter whole grains — and water instead of sweet drinks. Simple habits, big effect on glucose.

interview.title: Evidence Interview
interview.description: One question at a time — adapts to your answers

interview.patientHelper: Select the patient — answers we already know will be pre-filled.
interview.ageHelper: Age changes the thresholds we screen with.
interview.sexHelper: Biological sex — it decides which questions and thresholds apply.
interview.pregnantHelper: Pregnancy uses stricter blood-sugar thresholds — I will adjust if so.
interview.stageHelper: Gestational diabetes is usually screened between weeks 24–28.
interview.gdmPrevTitle: Have you had gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy?
interview.gdmPrevHelper: A previous episode raises lifetime risk and means earlier testing this time.
interview.onsetTitle: Did these symptoms come on suddenly?
interview.onsetHelper: Sudden onset (days to weeks) points to type 1 diabetes; a slow build-up over months or years points to type 2.
interview.coreSymptomsTitle: Which of these have you noticed recently?
interview.coreSymptomsHelper: Select all that apply — or tap "None of these" if you feel fine.
interview.otherSymptomsHelper: Select all that apply — or tap "None of these".
interview.warningTitle: Any of these warning signs right now?
interview.warningHelper: These help detect low blood sugar or emergencies.
interview.riskTitle: Do any of these apply to you?
interview.riskHelper: Answers already known from your health profile are pre-ticked — you can change them.
interview.bodyHelper: I will calculate BMI automatically — or enter it directly if you know it.
interview.hasLabsTitle: Do you have recent lab results?
interview.hasLabsHelper: Lab values sharpen accuracy a lot — but the interview works without them.
interview.labsTitle: Enter the lab values you have
interview.labsHelper: Any one of these helps — everything is optional, and ranges work too.
interview.extraTitle: Anything else to tell the clinician?
interview.extraHelper: Something the questions did not cover — optional.
interview.insightPregnantTitle: Pregnancy noted — adjusting what I check
interview.insightPregnantText: Gestational diabetes is screened with stricter thresholds. A couple of pregnancy questions follow, and your labs will be read against pregnancy ranges.
interview.insightT1dText: Weight loss together with intense thirst and frequent urination can point to type 1 diabetes, which can develop quickly. This will be flagged for clinician review.
interview.insightTriadText: Intense thirst, frequent urination and constant hunger together are the classic trio (polydipsia, polyuria, polyphagia) — high blood sugar pulls water out of your body. The next questions help me tell which type fits.
interview.insightT2Text: Symptoms that build up over months usually point to type 2 diabetes, where the body still makes insulin but resists it. Signs like dark skin patches, tingling and slow healing matter most here.
interview.insightChildTitle: In children this pattern is urgent
interview.insightChildText: Sudden thirst and urination in a child — especially with new bed-wetting — is a strong type 1 signal. A finger-prick glucose check today is the fastest way to know.
interview.insightKetosisText: Fruity breath or deep, rapid breathing can mean ketones are building up — a sign of insulin shortage. Combined with feeling unwell, this needs urgent medical attention.
interview.insightDkaText: Vomiting or stomach pain with high blood sugar can signal diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) — a medical emergency. If you feel very unwell right now, seek urgent care first; this assessment can wait.
interview.insightCheckTitle: Sign noted — the assessment keeps going
interview.insightCheckText: Stomach pain, vomiting, fruity breath or deep breathing can have many causes, and one sign on its own is not an emergency. The next questions help me tell whether this fits a pattern that needs urgent care.
interview.insightHypoText: Shakiness, sweating or dizziness can mean low blood sugar. If you have a glucose meter, a reading taken now would be valuable evidence.
interview.childProbeHelper: In children, new bed-wetting with extra thirst or urination is the strongest type 1 signal.
interview.t2ProbeHelper: With a slow build-up, these signs strongly point to the type 2 pattern.
interview.insightShortcutTitle: Skipping the lab questions — here is why
interview.insightShortcutText: With the signs you reported, the next step is the same no matter what a lab would say: get checked by a doctor today. I skipped the lab questions to save you time — finish the rest so your report is complete for the clinician.
interview.allAnsweredText: Review your evidence, then run the assessment.

diagnosisResult.hba1cSubtitle: A key marker of long-term glucose control.
diagnosisResult.fastingSubtitle: Indicates glucose level after an 8-hour fast.
diagnosisResult.symptomAlign: The patient's reported symptoms align with the matched diabetes pattern shown by the inference engine.
diagnosisResult.noSymptom: No prominent symptom pattern was selected.
diagnosisResult.noRisk: No risk factors were flagged in this submission.
diagnosisResult.noDetailedRule: No detailed rule reasoning is available for this run.
diagnosisResult.diagnosticReasoningP1: The system compares this assessment against structured diabetes rules from symptom, laboratory, and risk-factor evidence.
diagnosisResult.diagnosticReasoningP2: Confidence is calculated from the strength and priority of matched rules, then adjusted by evidence completeness.
diagnosisResult.diagnosticReasoningP3: This output is a decision-support summary and should be reviewed with a qualified healthcare professional.
diagnosisResult.preventionIntro: Healthy lifestyle choices can help prevent type 2 diabetes. If you have prediabetes, lifestyle changes may slow the condition or keep it from becoming diabetes.
diagnosisResult.preventionListIntro: A healthy lifestyle includes the following:
diagnosisResult.preventionEatText: Choose foods lower in fat and calories and higher in fiber. Focus on fruits, vegetables and whole grains.
diagnosisResult.preventionActiveText: Aim for 150 or more minutes a week of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity, such as brisk walking, bicycling, running or swimming.
diagnosisResult.preventionWeightText: If you are overweight, losing some weight and keeping it off may slow prediabetes from becoming type 2 diabetes. If you have prediabetes, losing 7% to 10% of your body weight may lower the risk of diabetes.
diagnosisResult.preventionSitText: Sitting for long periods can raise the risk of type 2 diabetes. Get up every 30 minutes and move around for at least a few minutes.
diagnosisResult.preventionMetformin: People with prediabetes may take metformin (Fortamet, Glumetza, others), a diabetes medicine, to lower the risk of type 2 diabetes. This is most often prescribed for older adults who are obese and who can't lower blood sugar levels with lifestyle changes.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmIntro: During pregnancy your blood-sugar targets are stricter. Gestational diabetes can usually be managed well — and its risks greatly reduced — with early care.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmWatchText: Test as your obstetric team advises. The 75g OGTT around weeks 24–28 confirms or rules out gestational diabetes — earlier if you have risk factors.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmEatText: Smaller, regular meals built on whole grains, vegetables and protein help avoid sugar spikes. Ask for a dietitian referral.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmActiveText: A short walk after meals lowers glucose spikes. Keep to the activity level your doctor approves for your pregnancy.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmFollowUpText: Gestational diabetes raises your lifetime type 2 risk. Re-test 4–12 weeks after delivery, then every 1–3 years.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmNote: Any diabetes treatment during pregnancy needs obstetric supervision — never start or stop medication on your own.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesIntro: Your results meet diabetes-level evidence. These steps protect your eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart — the earlier you start, the better.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesDoctorText: Bring these results with you. Diabetes treatment works best when it starts early — your doctor will set targets and a monitoring plan with you.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesLabsText: If you have not had one yet, a fasting glucose or HbA1c test confirms the result and becomes your baseline for tracking.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesBasicsText: The same lifestyle that prevents diabetes also treats it: healthy food, 150 minutes of activity a week, and a steady weight.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesCheckText: Ask your doctor about eye, kidney, foot and blood-pressure checks — catching problems early prevents lasting damage.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesNote: Urgent warning signs — vomiting, fruity breath, deep rapid breathing, or confusion — need emergency care straight away.
diagnosisResult.preventionRiskIntro: No diabetes yet — but your risk factors make prevention worthwhile. Small, steady changes cut the risk sharply.
diagnosisResult.preventionRiskMoveText: Brisk walking, cycling or swimming — anything that raises your breathing — is the single most effective habit.
diagnosisResult.preventionRiskWeightText: If you are overweight, losing 5–10% of your body weight measurably improves blood sugar and blood pressure.
diagnosisResult.preventionRiskFoodText: Build meals around vegetables, whole grains and lean protein; go easy on sugary drinks and processed snacks.
diagnosisResult.preventionRiskScreenText: With risk factors, screen for diabetes every 1–3 years — sooner if prediabetes is ever found.

plainSummary.title: In short
plainSummary.whatThisIs: This report compares your answers with common patterns of diabetes. It is a screening — not a final diagnosis. A doctor and a simple test can confirm.
plainSummary.matchedMany: Your answers matched {{count}} common sign(s) associated with high blood sugar.
plainSummary.matchedFew: This run included little direct evidence — the result leans on general risk patterns.
plainSummary.couldFitTwo: The signs could fit {{first}} ({{firstPercent}}%) or {{second}} ({{secondPercent}}%) — the first steps are the same either way.
plainSummary.noType: No single diabetes type pattern stood out yet.

excessiveThirst.meaning: Can occur when blood glucose is high — the body pulls water to dilute the sugar.
excessiveThirst.prevention: Drink water regularly and keep blood sugar in the target range; avoid sugary drinks.

frequentUrination.meaning: Often accompanies high blood glucose — the kidneys flush out the extra sugar.
frequentUrination.prevention: Limit caffeine in the evening and keep glucose well controlled to reduce night-time trips.

excessiveHunger.meaning: Can occur when glucose cannot effectively enter cells.
excessiveHunger.prevention: Eat balanced meals with fibre and protein so energy is released slowly.

weightLoss.meaning: The body burns fat and muscle for energy when glucose can't enter cells.
weightLoss.prevention: See a doctor soon — sudden weight loss needs checking; balanced meals help rebuild healthy weight.

fatigue.meaning: Cells don't get enough glucose for energy.
fatigue.prevention: Light regular exercise, good sleep and steady meals help restore energy.

blurredVision.meaning: High glucose draws water into the eye's lens, blurring focus.
blurredVision.prevention: Bring glucose back to target and get an eye exam — vision usually improves as sugar stabilises.

slowHealing.meaning: High glucose slows blood flow and weakens immune repair.
slowHealing.prevention: Clean and protect wounds early and keep glucose in range to speed up healing.

tingling.meaning: High glucose can irritate small nerve fibres over time.
tingling.prevention: Check your feet daily and keep glucose steady to protect the nerves from further damage.

frequentInfections.meaning: High glucose weakens the immune system's defences.
frequentInfections.prevention: Keep glucose in range, keep skin clean and dry, and treat infections early.

acanthosisNigricans.meaning: Dark, velvety skin patches — commonly linked with insulin resistance.
acanthosisNigricans.prevention: Weight loss and exercise often fade these patches — ask a doctor about insulin resistance.

irritability.meaning: Blood sugar swings can affect mood and concentration.
irritability.prevention: Steady meals, sleep and glucose control can lift mood — seek support if it persists.

recurrentInfections.meaning: Glucose in urine feeds bacteria and yeast.
recurrentInfections.prevention: Control sugar levels, stay hydrated, and see a doctor for infections that keep coming back.

bedWetting.meaning: Extra glucose pulls more water — a classic Type 1 sign in children.
bedWetting.prevention: A quick glucose check today can rule out early diabetes — see a doctor promptly.

fruityBreath.meaning: Possible diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) — seek care urgently.
fruityBreath.prevention: This can signal DKA (a dangerous chemical imbalance) — check ketones and seek urgent care.

deepRapidBreathing.meaning: The body tries to release ketone acids — seek care urgently.
deepRapidBreathing.prevention: An emergency sign (possible DKA) — go to emergency care immediately.

nausea.meaning: Can occur when blood glucose or ketones are very high.
nausea.prevention: Sip water slowly and seek care if it persists — nausea with high sugar can be serious.

vomiting.meaning: With very high glucose this can signal DKA — seek care urgently.
vomiting.prevention: Seek medical care quickly — vomiting with high glucose risks dehydration and DKA.

abdominalPain.meaning: With very high glucose this can signal DKA — seek care urgently.
abdominalPain.prevention: Get medical help promptly, especially with vomiting or high sugar — possible DKA.

sweating.meaning: Can be a warning sign of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia).
sweating.prevention: Check blood sugar — sweating can signal a low; keep fast-acting sugar within reach.

shaking.meaning: Common warning sign of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia).
shaking.prevention: Test glucose now — trembling often means low sugar; use the 15/15 rule if below 70 mg/dL.

dizziness.meaning: Can come from low — or very high — blood sugar.
dizziness.prevention: Sit down and check glucose; treat lows quickly and seek help if it is severe.

education.disclaimer: Educational background only — always follow your healthcare provider's advice.

general.name: diabetes
general.tagline: Blood sugar stays too high when the body can't make or use insulin well.
what: Insulin moves glucose (sugar) from your blood into your cells for energy.
With diabetes, the body makes little or no insulin, can't use it well, or both — so glucose builds up in the blood.
Over time, high blood glucose can harm the heart, kidneys, eyes, and nerves.
It can be managed — early treatment lowers the risk of complications.
symptoms: Feeling very thirsty or very hungry
Urinating more often, including at night
Tired all the time; blurry vision
Tingling or numb feet; sores that heal slowly
care: Confirm with lab tests: A1C, fasting glucose, or an oral glucose tolerance test.
Eat well, stay physically active, and keep a healthy weight.
Take prescribed medicines and monitor blood sugar as directed.
Get regular checkups for eyes, kidneys, nerves, and feet.

type1.name: Type 1 diabetes
type1.tagline: An autoimmune condition — the body makes little or no insulin.
what: The immune system mistakenly attacks the pancreas cells that make insulin.
Without insulin, glucose builds up in the blood instead of feeding your cells.
It often starts in children, teens, or young adults — but can appear at any age.
It is not caused by lifestyle, and it cannot be prevented.
symptoms: Very thirsty, very hungry, urinating often (including at night)
Losing weight without trying; tired all the time
Blurry vision; tingling in feet or hands
Emergency signs: deep rapid breathing, fruity breath, vomiting, stomach pain — seek care immediately
care: Daily insulin for life, by injection or an insulin pump.
Check blood glucose regularly (fingerstick or a wearable sensor).
Match insulin to food (carbohydrate counting) and activity.
Regular clinic visits to adjust doses and screen for complications.

type2.name: Type 2 diabetes
type2.tagline: The most common type — the body resists insulin.
what: Cells don't respond to insulin normally (insulin resistance), so glucose stays in the blood.
It develops slowly over years — many people feel fine at first.
Risk rises with excess weight, low activity, age over 35–45, and family history.
Healthy habits can control it — and sometimes prevent or delay it.
symptoms: Often no early symptoms — screening matters.
Numb or tingling hands and feet; sores that heal slowly
care: Healthy eating, regular activity, and weight management come first.
Medicines such as metformin are common; insulin can be added later.
Monitor blood glucose and A1C as your provider advises.
Yearly checks of eyes, kidneys, nerves, feet, and heart.

gestational.name: gestational diabetes
gestational.tagline: High blood sugar that develops during pregnancy.
what: Pregnancy hormones can block insulin, so blood sugar rises.
It usually appears midway through pregnancy and is found by screening at 24–28 weeks.
Most women feel no symptoms — that is why testing matters.
It often goes away after delivery, but it raises the chance of type 2 diabetes later.
symptoms: Usually none — detected by routine prenatal testing
Sometimes fatigue, blurred vision, or frequent infections
care: A healthy meal plan and regular gentle activity.
Check blood sugar at home as your provider directs.
Insulin or safe medicines if diet alone isn't enough.
Extra monitoring of the baby, and a glucose test after delivery.

prediabetes.name: prediabetes
prediabetes.tagline: Blood sugar is above normal — but not diabetes yet.
what: Glucose is higher than normal (A1C 5.7–6.4% or fasting 100–125 mg/dL).
Usually there are no clear symptoms — it is found through testing.
Without changes, it often progresses to type 2 diabetes.
Acting now can delay or even prevent type 2 diabetes.
symptoms: Some notice darkened, velvety skin patches on the neck or under the arms
care: Losing 5–7% of body weight greatly lowers the risk.
Aim for about 150 minutes of brisk activity each week.
Choose more vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein.
Recheck blood sugar at least once a year.

familyHistory.meaning: A parent or sibling with diabetes raises your lifetime risk — screening should start earlier and repeat regularly.

obesity.meaning: Excess body fat — especially around the waist — makes the body resistant to insulin, the top driver of type 2 diabetes.

overweight.meaning: A BMI of 25–30 already raises type 2 risk; a modest 5–10% weight loss brings it down sharply.

hypertension.meaning: High blood pressure often travels with high sugar and doubles the risk to the heart and kidneys.

sedentaryLifestyle.meaning: Sitting most of the day weakens glucose control — 150 minutes of movement a week cuts risk by about a third.

gestationalHistory.meaning: Diabetes during pregnancy means a high chance of type 2 later in life — test every 1–3 years.

smoking.meaning: Smoking worsens insulin resistance and damages blood vessels — quitting is the single best step.

highCholesterol.meaning: High cholesterol together with high sugar speeds up artery damage — diet, movement and medication help.

pcosHistory.meaning: PCOS is strongly linked to insulin resistance — women with PCOS need regular glucose checks.

ethnicityHighRisk.meaning: Some ethnic groups (South Asian, Southeast Asian and others) face higher risk at lower weights — screen earlier.
